# Background and Related Work {#sec-background}

The starting point for this project is a shift in how economists think about what technology displaces. @Autor2003 argued that technology does not replace occupations entirely, it replaces tasks. Work that adheres to explicit, rule-based procedures can be written down as a program, so computers substitute for it. On the other hand, work that demands judgment, adaptability, or situational response resists this translation and is instead complemented. By categorizing tasks along two axes, routine versus non-routine and cognitive versus manual, we can identify the four groups we use here. This approach transforms a vague concern about automation into a measurable concept.

Once exposure becomes measurable at the occupational level, it can be measured at the place level as well. This is because places differ in the types of work their residents do. @AutorDorn2013 demonstrated this by showing that local labor markets have long-lasting differences in their composition of work, which contributed to the polarization of employment across US commuting zones. Routine intensive areas experienced a decline in middle-wage jobs and an increase in employment at both the low and high ends of the wage distribution. Their occupation taxonomy is the one we use when categorizing occupations into task groups, and their finding that task composition is a persistent characteristic of a place, rather than a temporary feature of its residents, makes a panel design a sensible approach.

@AcemogluAutor2011 provided the formal basis for treating places this way. In their model, tasks serve as the production unit, and skill groups compete to supply them. Technology shifts which group holds the comparative advantage in which task. Consequently, local outcomes are influenced by the tasks performed in a local economy. This framework has become the standard for empirical research on automation and labor markets, and our county-level design incorporates its central assumption.

What this literature has not asked is what those wages actually buy in the places where workers live. Outcomes are reported in unadjusted wages and employment shares, so a high-wage metropolitan area and a low-wage rural county can appear vastly different in dollar terms even when the goods those wages purchase are comparable. Geography compounds the problem, since the commuting zone averages over the counties it encompasses and obscures the variation that determines whether a paycheck covers rent in any specific county. And because these relationships are typically estimated as linear ones, it remains largely unexplored whether affordability responds to task composition in fixed dollar increments or in a more gradual manner. None of this is a flaw in the previous work, which was intended to address different questions. Together, though, these three limit what it can say about county-level affordability.
